problem: Customers disliked late fees and Netflix offered rentals without them.
title: Blockbuster ends late fees and later reinstates them
context: Late fees were a major profit source and a common customer complaint for video rental stores.
decision_made: Eliminate late fees from 1 January 2005, selling the item to customers after a one-week grace period.
action_taken: Advertised "No Late Fees"; the company projected late fees would have contributed about $250 to $300 million to 2005 operating income.
observed_outcome: Attorneys general in dozens of states settled with Blockbuster over the "No Late Fees" advertising for about $630,000 in costs, and the company reported a second-quarter 2005 loss and retracted its 2005 guidance. Late fees were reinstated by 2010.
lessons: Giving up a major revenue stream for a marketing message can backfire if the terms are not clear and the business is already declining.
limitations: Coverage attributes the loss partly to wider industry decline. A $400 million loss figure and a Texas lawsuit were not confirmed and are not included.

claims.claim_text: Blockbuster announced it would drop late fees from 1 January 2005.
Attorneys general in many states settled with Blockbuster over its "No Late Fees" advertising.
Blockbuster reinstated late fees on video rentals in 2010.
